1014: Not a book but a process: Christian tradition holds that the church recognised, rather than created, the books God had inspired, testing them by apostolic origin, orthodoxy, antiquity and widespread use in worship.
1015: Historians describe a gradual process over roughly three centuries in which a core (four Gospels, Paul's letters, Acts, 1 Peter, 1 John) was settled by the late second century, while the edges (Hebrews, James, 2 Peter, 2-3 John, Jude, Revelation) remained disputed in some regions into the fourth century and beyond.
1016: Core NT collection in wide use (Irenaeus)
1018: Councils of Hippo / Carthage endorse 27 books in the West
1019: Council of Trent defines the Catholic canon dogmatically
1020: Readers asking why the Bible contains these books and not others, and why Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox Bibles differ in the Old Testament while agreeing on the New.
1021: From the Second Temple period, when the Hebrew Scriptures were read in three divisions and translated into Greek, through the apostolic letters circulating among churches, second-century controversies (Marcion, Gnostic gospels), fourth-century lists and councils, and the Reformation-era debates over the Old Testament Apocrypha.
1022: To trace, step by step, how the books of the Bible came to be received as Scripture, separating what the biblical text itself says from later church decisions and from scholarly reconstruction.
1023: Recognition rather than invention: the criteria of apostolicity, orthodoxy, antiquity and catholic (widespread) use
1024: The Old Testament the apostles read: Hebrew Scriptures and the Greek Septuagint
1026: Pressure from heresy (Marcion) and from persecution (which books to die for)
1027: Fourth-century lists: Eusebius, Athanasius, the African councils
1028: Why Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox Old Testaments differ
1029: Hebrew Bible / Tanakh: Law, Prophets and Writings
1030: Jesus speaks of the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms
1031: From Abel to Zechariah: first to last in the Hebrew order
1032: The 'Council of Jamnia' (c. 90) theory is now widely doubted; the Tanakh's limits were largely settled earlier
1033: Septuagint (3rd-2nd c. BC): the Greek Old Testament of the early church
1034: Translated in Alexandria; many NT quotations follow the Greek
1035: Its manuscripts also carry books outside the Hebrew canon (later called Apocrypha or deuterocanonical)
1037: Paul's letters read aloud and exchanged between churches
1038: Paul's letters already set beside 'the other Scriptures'
1039: Words of Jesus cited with Scripture
1040: Marcion (c. 144): a shortened canon provokes a response
1041: Rejects the Old Testament and its God; keeps an edited Luke and ten letters of Paul
1042: The church answers by affirming the OT and a wider apostolic collection
1043: Muratorian fragment (late 2nd c., some argue 4th c.)
1044: Lists four Gospels (Luke and John named), Acts, thirteen letters of Paul, Jude, two letters of John, Revelation
1045: Also accepts Wisdom of Solomon; mentions the Apocalypse of Peter as disputed; rejects the Shepherd of Hermas for public reading
1046: Silent on Hebrews, James and 1-2 Peter
1048: Argues there are four Gospels, no more and no fewer (Against Heresies 3.11.8)
1049: Appeals to apostolic succession and the rule of faith against Gnostic writings
1051: Uses all 27 books but notes doubts about Hebrews, James, 2 Peter, 2-3 John and Jude
1052: On Hebrews: the thoughts are Paul's, but who wrote it only God knows (reported by Eusebius, Church History 6.25)
1054: Recognised (homologoumena): four Gospels, Acts, Paul, 1 John, 1 Peter; Revelation 'if it seem proper'
1055: Disputed but known to most (antilegomena): James, Jude, 2 Peter, 2-3 John
1056: Spurious and heretical works rejected (Church History 3.25)
1057: Athanasius, 39th Festal Letter (367): first list of exactly our 27 NT books
1058: Calls them 'springs of salvation'; nothing to be added or taken away
1059: Commends some other books (Wisdom, Sirach, Esther, Judith, Tobit, Didache, Shepherd) for catechumens but not as canon
1060: Councils of Hippo (393) and Carthage (397): the West endorses 27 books
1061: Regional North African councils, influenced by Augustine; list includes the deuterocanonical OT books
1062: Jerome's Vulgate distinguishes Hebrew canon from 'church books' but includes them
1064: Responding to the Reformers, affirms 73 books (with the deuterocanonicals) as canonical
1065: Luther (1534) prints the Apocrypha in a separate section, 'useful and good to read' but not Scripture
1066: Protestant, Catholic and Orthodox differences today
1067: All three share the same 27-book New Testament
1068: Protestant OT follows the Hebrew canon (39 books); Catholic adds 7 deuterocanonical books plus additions to Esther and Daniel; Orthodox adds further books (1 Esdras, 3 Maccabees, Prayer of Manasseh, Psalm 151)
1069: Some churches keep wider or narrower canons: Syriac Peshitta (22 NT books), Ethiopian Orthodox (81 books)
1070: Jesus and the apostles already had Scripture: the Law, Prophets and Writings, read in Hebrew and Greek. Over the next three centuries the churches gathered the apostolic writings they had been reading in worship, argued over a handful of disputed books, and by the late fourth century converged on the same 27-book New Testament that Christians still share.
1071:
Three main canons exist today. The Protestant Bible has 66 books: a 39-book Old Testament matching the Hebrew Bible (Tanakh, counted as 24 books in Jewish reckoning) and the 27-book New Testament. The Catholic Bible has 73 books: it adds Tobit, Judith, 1-2 Maccabees, Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) and Baruch, plus Greek additions to Esther and Daniel, as defined at Trent (1546) following the Septuagint/Vulgate tradition and the African councils. Eastern Orthodox Bibles follow the Septuagint more fully and add 1 Esdras, 3 Maccabees, the Prayer of Manasseh and Psalm 151 (4 Maccabees often in an appendix); the Orthodox churches have not fixed the edges of the Old Testament by a single ecumenical decree.

All three agree on the 27-book New Testament, first listed exactly by Athanasius in 367. Smaller traditions differ at the edges: the Syriac Peshitta's 22-book New Testament omits 2 Peter, 2-3 John, Jude and Revelation, and the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo canon is broader still (including 1 Enoch and Jubilees). Protestants speak of the Apocrypha, Catholics and Orthodox of deuterocanonical books ("second canon"), and the difference turns on whether the church's Old Testament should follow the Hebrew canon or the church's historic Greek and Latin Bibles.
1074: Matthew (Levi) the tax collector and apostle. Papias (c. 120s, quoted by Eusebius, Church History 3.39.16) said Matthew compiled the sayings 'in the Hebrew dialect', and early church writers uniformly attribute the Gospel to him.
1075: The Gospel itself is anonymous. Most critical scholars hold that it was written in Greek by a Jewish-Christian teacher who used Mark and a sayings source (Q), which makes an eyewitness apostle seem less likely to them. Others argue the title tradition is early and unanimous, that Matthew may have been a source or patron of the work, and that Papias's remark may refer to Semitic style rather than language.
1076: Before the fall of Jerusalem (traditional and some conservative scholars)
1079: Jewish Christians, probably in Syria (Antioch is often suggested) or Galilee, living in tension with the synagogue after the destruction of the Temple.
1080: A community that kept the Law and the Jewish Scriptures but now confessed Jesus as Messiah and was drawing in Gentiles, in debate with emerging rabbinic leadership.
1081: To show that Jesus is the Messiah, Son of David and Son of Abraham, who fulfils the Law and the Prophets, to teach the community his commands in five great discourses, and to send it to make disciples of all nations.
1082: Fulfilment of Scripture ('this was to fulfil what was spoken')
1084: Jesus as the new Moses and authoritative teacher of the Law
1085: Righteousness that surpasses the scribes and Pharisees
1087: Mission to Israel widening to all nations
1088: Birth and infancy of the Messiah
1090: Magi, flight to Egypt, return to Nazareth
1091: Preparation and the Sermon on the Mount (discourse 1)
1094: Mighty works and the mission discourse (discourse 2)
1095: Rising opposition and the kingdom parables (discourse 3)
1096: Peter's confession and life in the community (discourse 4)
1097: You are the Christ; on this rock
1100: Jerusalem: conflict, woes and the Olivet discourse (discourse 5)
1103: End of the age and parables of judgment
1106: Empty tomb and commission to all nations
1107: Matthew opens the New Testament by tying Jesus to Abraham and David and presenting him as the one in whom Israel's story reaches its goal. He is Immanuel, God with us, at the start, and promises to be with his disciples to the end of the age as they carry his teaching to all nations.
1108: Matthew was the most quoted Gospel in the early church and stands first in almost every canon list and manuscript order; its place was never disputed.
1110: John Mark, companion of Paul, Barnabas and Peter, writing down Peter's preaching. Papias (quoted by Eusebius, Church History 3.39.15) says Mark was Peter's interpreter and wrote accurately, though not in order.
1111: The work is anonymous, but many scholars accept that a Mark wrote it, since attaching it to a minor figure would be an odd invention. Whether it depends directly on Peter is debated: some see Petrine eyewitness shaping (e.g. Bauckham), others see community traditions arranged by an author whose identity cannot be confirmed.
1112: Just after the fall of Jerusalem
1113: Early dating (a minority, e.g. J. Crossley)
1115: Largely Gentile Christians unfamiliar with Jewish customs (Mark explains them), traditionally in Rome; some scholars propose Syria or Galilee.
1116: A church facing suffering and possibly persecution, around the time of the Jewish War (66-70), needing to understand a crucified Messiah.
1117: To proclaim the good news of Jesus the Messiah, Son of God, showing that his authority is revealed in suffering and the cross, and calling readers to follow him on the way of the cross.
1118: Jesus as Son of God and suffering Son of Man
1119: The messianic secret and misunderstanding disciples
1120: Discipleship as taking up the cross
1122: The kingdom of God breaking in through exorcism and healing
1123: Prologue: John the Baptist, baptism, testing
1124: Ministry in Galilee: authority and controversy
1125: Calling of disciples and healings at Capernaum
1127: Parables and mighty works around the lake
1130: Feedings of five thousand and four thousand
1131: On the way: Peter's confession and three passion predictions
1132: You are the Christ; take up your cross
1133: The Son of Man came to serve and give his life a ransom
1134: Jerusalem: temple, controversy, the coming end
1137: The tomb is empty; the women flee afraid
1138: Longer ending (absent from the earliest manuscripts)
1139: Mark is the shortest and probably earliest Gospel, a fast-moving account in which Jesus' power is plain yet his identity is misunderstood until a Roman centurion at the cross calls him the Son of God. It ends abruptly at the empty tomb, leaving readers to answer the call to follow.
1140: Mark was accepted everywhere, though it was less quoted than Matthew. The ending is the main textual question: Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus end at 16:8, and most scholars regard 16:9-20 as a later addition, though some defend it and it remains in church lectionaries.
1142: Luke the physician, a companion of Paul, who also wrote Acts. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.1.1) and the Muratorian fragment name him.
1143: Almost all scholars agree Luke and Acts share one author. Many accept Luke the companion of Paul, pointing to the 'we' passages of Acts; others think the author was a later admirer of Paul, noting differences between Acts and Paul's letters. The author used Mark and other sources, as his preface says.
1144: Before Acts, written while Paul was still alive (c. 62)
1147: Theophilus, probably a Gentile patron, and through him a wider Greek-speaking, largely Gentile church.
1148: Churches spread across the Mediterranean needing an orderly, well-researched account linking Jesus to Israel's hopes and to the Gentile mission.
1149: To give Theophilus certainty about what he had been taught by setting out an orderly account of Jesus as Saviour for Israel and the nations, with special concern for the poor, women, outsiders and the work of the Spirit.
1150: Salvation for all: Jews, Samaritans, Gentiles, the poor and outcast
1152: Reversal: the humble lifted, the proud brought low
1153: Jerusalem as the goal of the journey
1157: Births of John and Jesus; Magnificat, Benedictus, Nunc Dimittis
1160: Nazareth manifesto: good news to the poor
1168: Luke's careful account, the first half of a two-volume work, follows Jesus from the temple in Jerusalem through Galilee and back to Jerusalem, where he dies and rises. Along the way he seeks and saves the lost, and he ends by opening the Scriptures and promising the Spirit for a mission to all nations.
1169: Luke was universally accepted. Marcion (c. 144) used an edited form of Luke as his only Gospel, which pushed other churches to affirm the full fourfold Gospel.
1171: John the son of Zebedee, identified with 'the disciple whom Jesus loved', writing in Ephesus in old age (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.1.1).
1172: The Gospel claims the witness of the Beloved Disciple (John 21:24) but does not name him. Many scholars see a multi-stage composition within a 'Johannine community', with the Beloved Disciple as its founding witness; some identify him with John the Elder mentioned by Papias rather than the apostle (e.g. Bauckham), and others still defend the son of Zebedee.
1174: Early dating before 70 (J. A. T. Robinson and others)
1175: Believers, and perhaps seekers, in a mixed Jewish and Gentile setting, traditionally Ephesus, some of whom had been expelled from the synagogue.
1176: Late first-century tension with synagogue leaders and questions about Jesus' identity, possibly alongside early docetic ideas.
1177: Stated explicitly: written so that readers may believe that Jesus is the Messiah, the Son of God, and by believing have life in his name.
1178: Jesus as the eternal Word made flesh
1182: Light and darkness, truth and falsehood
1183: The Spirit-Paraclete and love among disciples
1189: Man born blind and the Good Shepherd
1191: Farewell discourse in the upper room
1192: Foot washing and the new commandment
1193: Way, truth, life; the promised Spirit
1195: Book of Glory: passion and resurrection
1197: Mary Magdalene, the disciples and Thomas
1200: John begins before creation, with the Word who was with God and was God, and tells how that Word became flesh and revealed the Father's glory through signs, discourses and above all the cross. The book closes with a purpose statement inviting readers to believe and live.
1201: Some second-century groups favoured John (Valentinian Gnostics) and a few critics (the so-called Alogi) rejected it, but Irenaeus defended it as one of four Gospels and its place was secure by the late second century.
1204: Luke the physician, author of the Third Gospel and companion of Paul; the 'we' passages reflect his presence.
1205: Common authorship with Luke is nearly universal. Whether the author travelled with Paul is debated: supporters cite the 'we' passages and accurate local detail; critics note differences from Paul's letters (e.g. on the Jerusalem council and Paul's theology) and see a later idealising historian.
1206: Early date: written when the narrative ends, Paul still under house arrest
1208: Theophilus and the wider Gentile-majority church.
1209: A church that has spread from Jerusalem to Rome and needs to understand how a Jewish messianic movement became a multi-ethnic body, and how it stood before Roman authorities.
1210: To continue the story of what Jesus 'began to do and teach', showing the risen Lord at work by his Spirit as the witness spreads from Jerusalem to Judea, Samaria and the ends of the earth.
1215: God's sovereignty through opposition and imprisonment
1217: Programme: Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, ends of the earth
1220: Judea and Samaria: Philip, Saul, Cornelius
1224: Paul's first journey and the Jerusalem council
1225: Second and third journeys: Europe and Ephesus
1228: Ephesus and farewell to the elders
1229: Paul's arrest, trials and voyage to Rome
1230: Defences before Felix, Festus and Agrippa
1232: Acts tells how a small group of Jesus' followers in Jerusalem, filled with the Spirit at Pentecost, carried the message across the Roman world. It ends with Paul in Rome under house arrest, still proclaiming the kingdom of God boldly and without hindrance.
1233: Acts was accepted without serious dispute and is named in the Muratorian fragment as 'the acts of all the apostles'; Marcion rejected it. In many Greek manuscripts it is grouped with the Catholic (general) letters.
1236: The apostle Paul, dictating to Tertius (Rom 16:22).
1237: Undisputed: Romans is one of the seven letters virtually all scholars accept as Paul's. Debate concerns the integrity of chapter 16 and the two-chapter textual variations, not authorship.
1240: The church in Rome, a mixed congregation of Jewish and Gentile believers that Paul had not founded or yet visited.
1241: Written from Corinth near the end of the third journey, before Paul took the collection to Jerusalem and planned to go on to Spain. Jewish believers had returned after Claudius's expulsion (c. 49), possibly creating tension with a Gentile majority.
1242: To set out the gospel Paul preaches, to unite Jewish and Gentile believers, to explain God's faithfulness to Israel, and to gain support for his mission to Spain.
1243: The righteousness of God revealed in the gospel
1244: Universal sin and justification by faith
1245: Union with Christ and life in the Spirit
1247: Love and mutual welcome between strong and weak
1248: Greeting and theme: the gospel is God's power to save
1249: All have sinned: Gentile and Jew under judgment
1254: New life: freedom from sin, law and death
1257: Life in the Spirit; nothing can separate us
1259: Transformed minds and the body of Christ
1260: Strong and weak: welcome one another
1262: Romans is Paul's fullest explanation of his gospel: all humanity stands guilty, yet God has shown his righteousness by justifying through faith those who belong to Christ. He then shows how that gospel creates a new life in the Spirit, keeps faith with Israel and forms one worshipping people out of Jews and Gentiles.
1263: Accepted from the beginning in every list. Marcion's edition is reported to have lacked chapters 15-16, and some manuscripts place the closing doxology in different positions.
1265: The apostle Paul, with Sosthenes (1 Cor 1:1).
1266: Undisputed Pauline letter. Some propose that 1 Cor 14:34-35 is a later insertion and a few see editorial combination of letters, but authorship is not in doubt.
1268: The church Paul founded in Corinth, a prosperous Roman colony, made up mostly of Gentile converts of mixed social status.
1269: Written from Ephesus during the third journey after reports from Chloe's household and a letter of questions from Corinth.
1270: To heal divisions, correct moral and liturgical disorders, answer the church's questions on marriage, idol food, spiritual gifts and the resurrection, and recentre the church on Christ crucified.
1271: The wisdom of the cross versus worldly wisdom
1272: Unity of the church as one body
1274: Freedom limited by love for the weaker brother
1277: Divisions and the message of the cross
1278: Moral disorders: incest, lawsuits, sexual immorality
1279: Answers to their letter: marriage and singleness
1280: Food offered to idols and Christian freedom
1281: Worship: head coverings, the Lord's Supper, spiritual gifts
1285: The resurrection of Christ and of believers
1286: The gospel received: died, buried, raised, appeared
1289: Writing to a gifted but quarrelsome church, Paul answers practical problems one by one while bringing everything back to Christ crucified and risen. Along the way he gives the earliest written account of the Lord's Supper, the hymn to love and the oldest list of resurrection appearances.
1290: Accepted universally and quoted by Clement of Rome (1 Clement 47) in the 90s, among the earliest attested uses of any NT letter.
1292: The apostle Paul, with Timothy (2 Cor 1:1).
1293: Undisputed as Paul's. Many scholars think the canonical letter combines two or more letters (often chapters 1-9 and 10-13, sometimes with 6:14-7:1 and chapters 8 and 9 separated); others defend its unity.
1294: The church in Corinth and believers throughout Achaia.
1295: Written from Macedonia after a painful visit and a 'tearful letter'. Titus brought news of partial reconciliation, but rival 'super-apostles' were challenging Paul's authority.
1296: To complete reconciliation, explain his ministry of weakness and suffering, encourage generous giving to the Jerusalem collection, and defend his apostleship against opponents.
1298: The new covenant ministry of the Spirit
1299: Treasure in clay jars: power in weakness
1300: Reconciliation with God and one another
1302: Comfort and Paul's change of plans
1303: The ministry of the new covenant
1306: New creation and the ministry of reconciliation
1310: Thorn in the flesh: my grace is sufficient
1311: 2 Corinthians is Paul's most personal letter. He opens his heart to a church that had doubted him and argues that true apostolic ministry looks like Christ's: marked by suffering and weakness, yet carrying God's power and the message of reconciliation.
1312: Accepted universally, though it is less clearly cited than 1 Corinthians in the earliest Fathers. It is listed in Marcion's collection and the Muratorian fragment.
1314: The apostle Paul, writing partly in his own hand (Gal 6:11).
1315: Undisputed Pauline letter; it is a cornerstone for reconstructing Paul's life and thought.
1316: South Galatian theory, before the Jerusalem council
1317: North Galatian theory, during the Ephesian ministry
